Vectors in West and Central Africa of filarial worm *Loa loa* (eye worm)
Filarial worms reside in the subcutaneous tissues, lymphatic system, or body cavities of humans.
Wolbachia spp., an endosymbiotic bacterium in filarial worms, contributes to pathogenesis by inducing inflammatory responses.

qs.q: Which morphological feature distinguishes male filarial worms from female filarial worms?
qs.e: Male filarial worms possess perianal papillae and unequal spicules but lack a caudal bursa. In contrast, female worms are longer and viviparous.

qs.q: A research team studies a species of filarial worm whose microfilariae exhibit peak circulation in peripheral blood during daylight hours. What is this periodicity called?
qs.e: Diurnal periodicity refers to microfilariae that exhibit peak circulation during the day, such as Loa loa. Nocturnal periodicity features peak circulation at night.

qs.q: A patient presents with scrotal swelling due to fluid accumulation caused by lymphatic obstruction from adult filarial worms. What is this clinical feature called?
qs.e: Hydrocele is the accumulation of fluid in the scrotum due to lymphatic obstruction. Chyluria refers to lymph in the urine rather than fluid in the scrotum.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Filarial worms are parasitic nematodes that live in subcutaneous tissue, lymphatics, or body cavities. They are transmitted by insect vectors and cause a spectrum of chronic inflammatory diseases. Understanding their life cycle and host response guides diagnosis and treatment.

sections.p: Filarial worms are long, thread‑like nematodes that depend on an insect vector to reach humans. Adult worms reside in specific body sites, releasing microfilariae that circulate in blood or skin.
b: Major species: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Loa loa, Onchocerca volvulus, Mansonella perstans

sections.p: Adult filariae are 30‑100 cm long, with a sheath that protects microfilariae. They lack a digestive tract and obtain nutrients from the host via surface absorption.
b: Microfilariae are sheathed (W. bancrofti, B. malayi) or unsheathed (Loa loa)
Sexual dimorphism: females larger, produce thousands of microfilariae daily

sections.p: Infected insects ingest microfilariae during a blood meal; the parasite undergoes development to infective L3 larvae, which are transmitted to a new host during the next bite.
b: Culex, Anopheles, Aedes – transmit lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti, B. malayi)
Chrysops spp. – transmit Loa loa (eye worm) in West/Central Africa

sections.p: Clinical disease depends on worm location: lymphatic obstruction (elephantiasis), subcutaneous migration (Loa loa), ocular involvement (onchocerciasis), or systemic symptoms from massive microfilaremia.
b: Lymphatic filariasis: chronic lymphedema, hydrocele, genital swelling
Loiasis: transient eye migration, Calabar swellings, pruritus
Onchocerciasis: skin depigmentation, intense itching, river blindness

sections.p: Diagnosis combines clinical clues with detection of microfilariae, antigen tests, and imaging when needed.

t.a: Peripheral blood smear (night‑time for W. bancrofti)
t.b: Does the patient have circulating microfilariae? Positive smear confirms active infection; negative does not rule out if timing is wrong.
Is adult W. bancrofti present? Positive antigen indicates active adult infection even when microfilariae are absent.
Are microfilariae present in skin? Positive confirms onchocerciasis; negative may need repeat or PCR if suspicion high.
Is there live adult worm movement in lymphatics? Visualizes adult worms, useful when labs unavailable.

sections.p: Therapy targets microfilariae first, then adult worms, while managing inflammation and preventing complications.
b: Microfilaricidal drugs: diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for loiasis and lymphatic filariasis; ivermectin for onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis (where DEC contraindicated).
Adulticidal drug: doxycycline (10‑14 days) to eradicate Wolbachia, leading to sterility and death of adult worms.
Supportive care: limb hygiene, compression, surgery for hydrocele, eye protection in onchocerciasis.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: Night‑time blood draw is essential for detecting W. bancrofti microfilariae.
Loa loa can cause severe encephalopathy after DEC; use ivermectin cautiously.
Wolbachia elimination with doxycycline improves long‑term outcomes and reduces adverse reactions to microfilaricidal drugs.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive swelling causing airway or urinary obstruction

faq.q: Why do some filarial infections cause itching while others do not?
faq.a: Itching results from immune reaction to microfilariae in the skin (e.g., onchocerciasis) or subcutaneous migration (Loa loa). Lymphatic filariasis mainly causes swelling, not itch.

faq.q: Can filarial infections be cured completely?
faq.a: Adult worms can be sterilized or killed with doxycycline; microfilariae are cleared with DEC or ivermectin, leading to long‑term remission, but reinfection is possible.

faq.q: Is a single dose of ivermectin enough for onchocerciasis?
faq.a: Ivermectin kills microfilariae but not adult worms; repeated annual dosing is required to suppress transmission.
